snip.t: Generally, upper motor neuron signs are not present, seizures are uncommon, and intellect is preserved in many patients.
“How would you differentiate an upper motor neuron from a lower motor neuron lesion on exam?” (Spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski vs. flaccidity, fasciculations, atrophy)
Reflexes: Deep tendon reflexes, Babinski sign, clonus — Upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar) confirm supratentorial corticospinal involvement.

Motor exam (strength grading, tone): Upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski) indicate cord involvement above the level of the lesion; lower motor neuron signs (flaccidity, fasciculations) suggest anterior horn cell or nerve root compression.
Motor weakness (upper motor neuron pattern): Compression of corticospinal tracts by a mass or edema.
Brainstem region tumors may be associated with gaze palsy, cranial nerve palsies, and upper motor neuron deficits (hemiparesis, hyperreflexia, and clonus).
Definition: Progressive loss of upper motor neurons (cerebral cortex) AND lower motor neurons (spinal cord + brainstem) → muscle denervation → weakness
